hints: Think about which classic test uses alkaline aqueous iodine and gives a yellow solid when the molecule contains a $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}$ group.
walkthrough:
Spot the test from the reagents**
You see alkaline aqueous iodine plus a yellow precipitate. That combination is famous. It is the triiodomethane test for methyl carbonyl type groups, $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ or $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}$.

Name the yellow solid**
The yellow precipitate itself is always the same compound, $\text{CHI}_3$. Its systematic name is triiodomethane, commonly called iodoform.
Final answer: Triiodomethane (iodoform), $\text{CHI}_3$.

hints: Count the longest carbon chain in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and number to give the $\text{OH}$ group the lowest possible number.
walkthrough:
Name the alcohol systematically**
Look at $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. There are four carbons in a row, so the parent is butane. The $\text{OH}$ is on carbon 2, and it is a secondary alcohol. So the name is butan-2-ol.
Final answer: Butan-2-ol.

hints: X is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ as an alcohol. Think how the $\text{OH}$ can move to carbon 1 and how the carbon skeleton can branch.
Remember you need three new alcohols, so look for butan-1-ol, a branched primary alcohol, and a branched tertiary alcohol.
walkthrough:
Keep the same formula, change the structure**
X is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$. To make structural isomers that are still alcohols, keep four carbons and one $\text{OH}$, but rearrange the skeleton or the $\text{OH}$ position.

Draw the three missing alcohols**
First, move $\text{OH}$ to the end of the straight chain: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, butan-1-ol. Second, branch the chain with $\text{OH}$ on a primary carbon: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{OH}$, 2-methylpropan-1-ol. Third, branch the chain with $\text{OH}$ on the central carbon: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, which is tertiary.

Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ (butan-1-ol) and $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{OH}$ (2-methylpropan-1-ol) and $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$ (2-methylpropan-2-ol).

hints: Compare $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ with $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and notice what happens to the $\text{C-OH}$ group.
walkthrough:
See loss of hydrogen as oxidation**
In reaction 1 the $\text{CH(OH)}$ group becomes $\text{C=O}$. The molecule loses hydrogen from the carbon and the oxygen, and gains a carbon oxygen double bond. A secondary alcohol to a ketone is oxidation.
Final answer: Oxidation (redox).

hints: Recall the standard orange to green oxidising agent used to oxidise secondary alcohols to ketones under heating.
walkthrough:
Pick the AS oxidant for alcohol to carbonyl**
For a controlled oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone you use dichromate(VI) in acid, heated. That means acidified potassium dichromate(VI) or acidified sodium dichromate(VI). The orange solution turns green as it reacts.
Final answer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) or sodium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ / $\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ with $\text{H}^+$ / $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.

hints: Reaction 2 removes $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from butan-2-ol to give $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$. Think where the double bond can form.
Draw but-1-ene from loss of a hydrogen on carbon 1, and but-2-ene from loss of a hydrogen on carbon 3.
Remember but-2-ene can exist as two stereoisomers because each $\text{C}$ of the $\text{C=C}$ carries two different groups.
walkthrough:
Understand dehydration**
Passing the vapour over hot aluminium oxide removes water from the alcohol. This is elimination. From $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ you can remove $\text{OH}$ from carbon 2 plus $\text{H}$ from either carbon 1 or carbon 3.

Form the two positional isomers**
If $\text{H}$ is lost from carbon 1, the double bond is at the end: $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, but-1-ene. If $\text{H}$ is lost from carbon 3, the double bond is in the middle: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$, but-2-ene.

Split but-2-ene into cis and trans**
In but-2-ene each carbon of the $\text{C=C}$ is joined to $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{H}$. Restricted rotation about the double bond gives two stereoisomers: cis-but-2-ene (Z) with both $\text{CH}_3$ groups on the same side, and trans-but-2-ene (E) with them on opposite sides. Together with but-1-ene that makes three isomers.
Final answer: But-1-ene and cis-but-2-ene (Z-but-2-ene) and trans-but-2-ene (E-but-2-ene).

hints: Start with the $\text{C=C}$ electrons attacking the $\delta+$ end of $\text{HBr}$. Identify which atom of $\text{HBr}$ is $\delta+$.
Think which carbocation forms when $\text{H}^+$ adds to $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CCH}_2$: a primary or a tertiary cation.
Show the $\text{H-Br}$ bond breaking to give $\text{Br}^-$ in the first step.
Finish by showing the lone pair on $\text{Br}^-$ forming the new $\text{C-Br}$ bond to the positive carbon.
walkthrough:
Set up the electrophile**
$\text{HBr}$ is polar because $\text{Br}$ is more electronegative than $\text{H}$, so label it $\text{H}^{\delta+}\text{Br}^{\delta-}$. The $\text{C=C}$ in methylpropene, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=CH}_2$, is electron rich and will attack $\text{H}^{\delta+}$.

Show the first curly arrows**
Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C=C}$ double bond to the $\text{H}$ of $\text{HBr}$. At the same time draw a curly arrow from the $\text{H-Br}$ bond onto $\text{Br}$ to make $\text{Br}^-$. The $\text{H}$ joins the $\text{CH}_2$ end to give the more stable cation.

Draw the tertiary carbocation intermediate**
Adding $\text{H}^+$ to the terminal $\text{CH}_2$ leaves the positive charge on the central carbon: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$. This is a tertiary carbocation, with the $+$ carbon joined to three methyl groups. Show the $+$ charge clearly.

Attack by bromide**
Now show $\text{Br}^-$ with its lone pairs. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{Br}^-$ to the $\text{C}^+$ to form the $\text{C-Br}$ bond. This gives 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}$.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{C=C}$ curly arrow to $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{H}^{\delta+}\text{Br}^{\delta-}$; $\text{H-Br}$ bond curly arrow to $\text{Br}$ to form $\text{Br}^-$ and $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$ tertiary carbocation. Step 2: lone pair on $\text{Br}^-$ curly arrow to $\text{C}^+$ to give 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

hints: Compare the two possible carbocations from addition of $\text{H}^+$ to the two ends of the double bond: tertiary versus primary.
Think how alkyl groups push electron density toward the positive carbon and why more alkyl groups means greater stabilisation.
walkthrough:
Link product to intermediate stability**
The major product comes from the lower energy pathway. Addition of $\text{H}^+$ to give the tertiary cation $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$ is much more favourable than addition to give the primary cation $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2^+$. So the tertiary route dominates.

Explain stability with inductive effect**
Alkyl groups are electron releasing by the positive inductive effect. Three methyl groups push more electron density onto the $\text{C}^+$ and spread the positive charge more effectively than one alkyl group. That extra stabilisation makes the tertiary carbocation form faster, so 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is the major product.

Final answer: The tertiary carbocation intermediate is more stable than the primary carbocation.
This is due to the positive inductive electron releasing effect of more alkyl (methyl) groups.
